lines.text: This is a Foray about the history of barbecue. Much of what you'll hear is written by AI. We work hard to get the facts right, but AI gets things wrong — so take it as a starting point, not a source.

Barbecue is a trade: it turns cheap, tough protein into abundance using fire, smoke and hours instead of cash. Follow the fire and you get technique — combustion, collagen, the chemistry of smoke, the difference between a skewer over coals and a pit dug into the ground. The traditions resemble each other because they are independent answers to the same physics, and the local variables are fuel, animal and faith.

Follow the labour instead and you get history. Because the hours are long, barbecue cannot be one person's weekday dinner; it needs a crowd, so it becomes an institution. And because those hours are hot and punishing, every barbecue culture has to answer the question of who tends the fire — which is always, underneath, a question about who holds power and who gets the credit.

Six names the narrator has to get right. In Japan the charcoal is binchōtan. In Yucatán the pit is a barbacoa. On the Argentine parrilla it is an asado, and in South Africa the same fire is a braai. The Quechua word for dried, salted meat is ch'arki, and the Taíno of the Caribbean gave the technique the word we still use.
